results.title: Amazon launches a faster Fire TV Stick 4K with a new remote design
results.author: Alina Maria Stan
results.content:
Amazon has launched a faster Fire TV Stick 4K with a redesigned remote, running its own Vega operating system rather than Android. That switch also removes sideloading, and the Digital Markets Act cannot require Amazon to restore it, because none of its operating systems is designated.
Amazon has launched the Fire TV Stick 4K, which it says reaches content 20 to 40% faster than a rival stick at a similar price. It comes with a redesigned remote and shipped today in Britain, Germany, France, Italy and Spain. It cannot install apps from outside Amazon’s store.
The remote has an asymmetric shape, a metal home button and a customisable star button, and sells alone for $14.99. The stick drops Android for Amazon’s Vega system, and 9to5Google reported that Vega kills sideloading.
Amazon’s announcement does not mention that. It told The Athletic the switch was to support creators and protect customers, because piracy can expose users to malware and fraud. Its public statement cites only flexibility.
In Europe that removal is lawful, because of what Amazon is not. The Digital Markets Act obliges gatekeepers to open designated operating systems to rival software.
Article 6(4) says a gatekeeper “shall allow and technically enable the installation and effective use of third-party software applications or software application stores” on its operating system. Hence sideloaded app stores on iPhones here.
Amazon is a designated gatekeeper, but only two of its services carry the label, Amazon Marketplace and Amazon Advertising. Neither is an operating system.
Apple tried to have its designation read narrowly and lost its EU court challenge in July. Its iOS and iPadOS stay listed, with Alphabet’s Android Mobile and Microsoft’s Windows.
Amazon has no operating system among the 23 designated services, so Article 6(4) cannot reach Fire TV in any member state.
Price is the other half. Amazon raised device prices overnight in August, taking the 4K Max from $60 to $85. The new 4K arrives at $59.99, the Max’s old price.
Amazon blamed memory and storage costs. The new stick has 8 GB of storage, and Americans can have it for $29.99 during Prime Big Deal Days.
Its European exposure is growing elsewhere. The Commission signalled in June that AWS and Azure appear to meet the gatekeeper test, with a decision due this year.
Alexa+ ships on the stick and runs on Fire TV in 11 countries. The AI Act has required since 2 August that people be told when they deal with an AI system.
Amazon has removed a capability from a device it sells across the EU, just as the same one is forced onto its rivals. Whether the Commission examines Fire TV is the open question.

results.summary:
Amazon has launched a new Fire TV Stick 4K featuring the proprietary Vega operating system, which improves performance speeds but restricts users from sideloading third-party applications.

### Key Points
- The new Fire TV Stick 4K runs on the Vega OS, replacing the previous Android-based software used by Amazon.
- Amazon claims the device loads content 20 to 40% faster than competing streaming sticks at similar price points.
- The redesigned remote features an asymmetric shape, a metal home button, and a customizable star button.
- Sideloading is disabled on the new system, a move Amazon states is intended to protect users from malware and piracy.
- Because Amazon’s operating systems are not designated as "gatekeepers" under the EU Digital Markets Act, the company is not legally required to allow third-party app stores.
- The device is currently available in Britain, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain, with a U.S. promotional price of $29.99 during Prime Big Deal Days.

### Why it Matters
This transition to a closed operating system highlights Amazon's strategy to exert greater control over its hardware ecosystem while avoiding the interoperability mandates currently imposed on rivals like Apple and Google. By bypassing Digital Markets Act requirements, Amazon maintains a walled garden that could influence future regulatory scrutiny regarding its cloud and advertising services.

results.title: At the Money: The Data Behind America’s Wealthy
results.author: Barry Ritholtz
results.content:
At the Money: The Data Behind America’s Wealthy with Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick (September 30, 2026)
In this episode of ‘At the Money,’ I speak with Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick about the data behind America’s wealthiest people. About this week’s guests: Owen Zidar is professor of Economics and Public Affairs at Princeton, and Eric Zwick is professor of Economics and Finance at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. Their new book is “The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There.”
Full transcript below. Part 1 is here.
~~~
A dozen data points from the book:
1. The 1-to-1,000 Ratio (Public CEOs vs. Private Owners) For every single CEO of a large, publicly traded company in America, there are more than 1,000 private business owners with at least $25 million in net worth.
2. Main Street Wealth Swamps the Forbes 400: The Forbes 400 list receives 50% of all news coverage on wealth, its members hold only about 3% of total US household wealth. “Main Street Millionaires” hold more than 13 times the wealth of the Forbes 400—accounting for roughly 40% of all household wealth in the United States.
3. Nearly 5 Million Households Have Over $5 Million; they are the top 4%
2 million decamillionaires ($10M+) and
65,000 centimillionaires ($100M+).
4. Wealth Drives Business Ownership Rates Equity in a business is dominant vehicle for extreme wealth.
5. Half of Americans worth $5 million own a private business; at $10 million, that figure climbs to three-quarters; and above $100 million, virtually everyone owns a private business.
6. Private Owners Out-Earn Public C-Suite Executives 15-to-1 2022, America’s 9,000 top public company C-suite executives earned a collective $38 billion. By contrast, the top 1% of private business owners (a group 10 times as large) earned $570 billion—private owners collectively earned 15X times as much. Individually, average private owner in the top 1% earned 1.5 times as much as the average public CEO.
6B. 70 Cents of Every Pass-Through Dollar Goes to the Top 1% Tax Reform Act of 1986: 95% of all U.S. businesses reorged into pass-through structures (S-corps, LLCs, partnerships) to avoid double taxation.
7. Today, 70 cents of every $1 in pass-through business profits flows directly to households in the top 1% of income.
8. $200 Billion Transferred Tax-Free Every Year $30 million per married couple 2025 and sophisticated estate-planning tools, only 0.1% of all U.S. estates pay any federal estate tax. Americans pass on $200B annually tax-free.
9. The $100 Million Age (20 to 60): Accumulating top-tier wealth takes long horizons of reinvestment.
10. To reach the top 0.1% in wealth for your age group, a person needs:
in their 20s $9.6 million
in their 40s, $41.8 million;
in their 60s, $112.4 million—almost 6 times as much as someone in their 30s.
11. The $300 Billion Noncompete Penalty Over 20% of American workers are subject to noncompete agreements, which restrict employees from switching to local competitors or starting their own firms. Banning noncompete agreements nationwide would boost comp by $300B annually.
12. Overrepresentation of Wealth in Congress: Decamillionaires are 10X + as likely to sit in Congress as general population; centimillionaires are 62X as likely. Between 25% and 50% of federal lawmakers are private business owners or practice-owning professionals, giving biz interests significant sway over tax and regulatory policy
~~~

TRANSCRIPT:
AT THE MONEY: The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America
Barry Ritholtz with Owen Zidar (Princeton) and Eric Zwick (University of Chicago)
Bloomberg Audio · Part Two
BARRY RITHOLTZ: America is a rich nation. But I want to get granular as to exactly how rich, who is rich, and how they got that way. The data is astounding. To help us unpack all of this and what it might mean for your personal prosperity, let’s bring in Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick. They’re professors at Princeton and the University of Chicago, respectively, and they are the authors of a fascinating new book, The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There.
And if you’re listening to this, be sure and check out part one, where we discuss a lot of the findings in the book. Today I really want to talk about the data, which really is very mind-blowing. Let’s start out with the thousand-to-one ratio, private owners versus public CEOs. For every wealthy CEO, there are more than a thousand private business owners worth at least $25 million in net worth. That blew my mind. Tell me a little bit about that.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: Yeah, so it’s a great statistic. It started out when we were thinking about the pass-through income and the growth of pass-throughs. Let’s add up all the income for top 1% pass-through business owners. And what’s a good reference for that, to make the point that this is a huge, surprisingly huge group? Well, let’s look at CEOs in the executive comp data set, which is roughly the S&P 1500, and it takes the CEOs, the CFOs, and adds up their salary plus the market values of their options.
And you say, okay, add that up. And it turns out they’re just swamped in size by the pass-through income flows for the pass-through business owners, because there are just way more of them, and they’re all across the industry, all across the country. You know, we’re talking about 1,500 CEOs plus another thousand CFOs or top execs, and we’re talking about over a million of these top 1 to 0.5% business owners.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: A million and a half people worth $25 million or more who are not running public companies. It’s amazing. Let’s talk about something even more finite: the Forbes 400. You guys explain how much Main Street swamps the Forbes 400. The Forbes 400 list receives 50% of all news coverage on wealth; its members hold only 3% of total US household wealth.
Meanwhile, Main Street millionaires are worth 13 times more than the total combined wealth of the Forbes 400, accounting for 40% of all household wealth. That data is just mind-blowing, especially how lopsided the media coverage is on the billionaires in the Forbes 400.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: To us, that’s one of the main points of the book. When you think about, you know, how to get rich or the influence of the rich in America, there’s just such a monopoly on attention on a very small handful of people, and we want to broaden the aperture to say, look, there’s a lot of money in America. It’s a very rich place with a lot of opportunity, and it’s not just the Forbes 400. We need to broaden it when we’re thinking about opportunity, tax policy, and, you know, just a huge range of issues that people care about. And we really think the narrative needs to be reset.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I want to really get granular with the data and just reveal how far off the narrative is. 5 million households have over $5 million. That’s the top 4%. And if you’ve followed the Fidelity 401(k) millionaire data, that really shouldn’t be a terrible surprise.
But then there are 2 million Americans worth $10 million or more. And then the number that I think could be the most shocking number in the entire book: if you ask people how many people are worth a hundred million or more in America, I don’t know, they’d say a few hundred, a few thousand. 65,000 Americans are centimillionaires, worth more than a hundred million dollars. I think that was the most shocking number in the entire book.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: It’s a huge group of people. So the 400 is 400 people. If you add all the people in their families, their kids, maybe it’s 1,500 people or 2,000 people — not 65,000. Right? So we’re talking about 30 to, you know, 50 times the number of people here.
That’s why not only are there a lot of $3 or $4 million houses, but there are a lot of $10, $20 million houses. That’s why in Aspen the average house price is so high. It’s not just some tech people from Silicon Valley buying those houses. It’s car dealers and people running manufacturing businesses making inputs into production for construction and so on.
And they’ve accumulated really screw-you money, and it’s amazing.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, I always say if you want to feel really bad about yourself, go to Zillow, set it to sold houses, and look at a wealthy part of America, out in the Hamptons. It’s genuinely shocking how many $30, $40, $50 million houses — hundreds — transact every summer. It blows my mind. Here’s another data point that I’m kind of starting to intuit, having plowed through the book: half of Americans worth $5 million or more own a private business.
That really seems to be the data point that is the core theme here: if you want to accumulate that sort of wealth, or you want to understand where that wealth is in America, you have to look at business owners.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: That’s absolutely right. One of the things that really jumped out to us when we were looking at pass-through businesses is that 70 cents of every dollar of income of these entities went to the top 1%. So this is really much more concentrated than public equity ownership and other forms of wealth, and it’s just very prevalent as you go further and further up into the wealth distribution.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: And again, more confirmation bias for me. I’m fond of saying the only reason any family should ever pay estate tax is if, on the way to your attorney to sign the documents, you’re hit by a bus. And you guys confirm that, because $200 billion transfers tax-free every year. Only 0.1% of all US estates pay any estate tax. That’s down — I did an analysis on that 15 years ago, and I want to say it was 0.4%, so it’s even less today.
Tell us a little bit about hundreds of billions of dollars transferring tax-free every year.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: And it’s quite striking. I mean, one of the reasons why I think it’s fallen is that the threshold has moved from $1.2 million in the early 2000s up to $30 million for married couples, and so we’ve really decimated it. There’s also a huge range of avoidance schemes. I think Gary Cohn, who was the NEC director in the first Trump administration, said only morons pay the estate tax.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s true. So it’s really amazing. Go on.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: Yeah, so I think, you know, this is one area where, if you look at what happened to the estate tax, a lot of it was basically sold on, “Oh, we need to help the little guy.” And there were some really wealthy business owners who were kind of using that to decimate it. And given how much wealth is transferring with the great wealth transfer, I think it’s high time to revisit the estate and inheritance tax regime, because it’s really amazing how little we collect in estate taxes.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: I want to talk about something that’s sort of contra to the main theme. You discuss some issues that can address some of that K shape we talked about, some of the inequalities that are there. I knew that there was a labor penalty for all these non-competes that are out there. I had no idea it was $300 billion annually.
Some states allow it; some states, like California, do not. If we were to get rid of all these non-competes — and I’m not talking about where there are very specific trade secrets, just run-of-the-mill non-competes for people who are just doing their daily jobs and are not senior and have no access to that — $300 billion a year. We’d go a long way to closing that K a little bit. Tell us about why we should get rid of all these non-competes.
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: So we try and place, you know, these Everywhere Millionaires and the businesses they run in this broader conversation about what’s going on with the labor share — what’s going on with the share of overall economic activity that’s going to workers versus owners — and suggest that some of the same factors that I think have gotten a lot more attention, which is, you know, workers having fewer options in terms of where to go if they’re not being treated well at a given employer… That’s, I think, a story that’s been told for large public companies maybe, but not so much for these smaller companies. And it turns out that non-competes are really broad and have expanded.
You see a Jimmy John’s or a Jersey Mike’s applying non-competes to the sandwich artists, and, you know, there is a lot of artistry in making a hoagie, and I have a taste for one as lunch approaches, but you shouldn’t be restricted from leaving one Jimmy John’s to go across the street to make sandwiches for somebody else. And if you scale that up, you know, the ability to walk out the door as a worker is a lot of power to get better wages as the company’s doing well. And these things have really proliferated in a way that seems kind of unhelpful for the conversation on inequality, and unnecessary, I think, when we think about, you know, protecting the secret to making that perfect sandwich.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Last question, which I guess indirectly relates to that. When you guys looked at wealth to see how overrepresented wealthy congressmen are versus the general public, the numbers are kind of shocking. So the decamillionaires, people worth $10 million, are 10x as likely — 10 times as likely — to sit in Congress as they’re found in the general population. But where this is really egregious is with the group of people worth a hundred million or more, the centimillionaires: you’re 62 times more likely to sit in Congress than you are to be found in the general population.
Tell us how that came about, and what does that mean for policy and income and wealth inequality?
OWEN ZIDAR & ERIC ZWICK: Yeah, it’s really quite striking. If you go to the grocery store, one out of every 33 people you meet is a private business owner. If you go to Congress, it’s one out of four. And I think some of that is because of the role of wealth and how hard it is to raise money.
And so if you think about who is the senator, or who’s playing golf with the senator, you know, it’s a lot of these folks. And the consequences are really quite striking in terms of thinking about who represents us when you’re making decisions about the deficit or debt, and, you know, some of these large tax bills that come through. I think that’s one part of the story for why we’ve seen such growth in their wealth: there are a lot of small loopholes that have kind of avalanched over time in recent decades, as a consequence of being so well represented, both in terms of people and in terms of their interests.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: To wrap up: if you are interested in either understanding wealth in America or becoming wealthy in America, The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There by Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick is the book for you. I found it fascinating, and I think you will also. I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Bloomberg’s At The Money.
results.summary:
In their new book, "The Everywhere Millionaire," economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick analyze data revealing that private business owners hold significantly more U.S. wealth than public CEOs.

### Key Points
- Private business owners with at least $25 million in net worth outnumber public company CEOs by a ratio of more than 1,000-to-1.
- "Main Street" millionaires collectively hold 13 times more wealth than the entire Forbes 400 list, accounting for roughly 40% of total U.S. household wealth.
- There are approximately 65,000 centimillionaires in the U.S., individuals with a net worth exceeding $100 million.
- Private business ownership is the primary driver of extreme wealth, with nearly 75% of individuals worth $10 million or more owning a private firm.
- Federal estate tax exemptions have risen to $30 million for married couples, allowing $200 billion to be transferred tax-free annually.
- Centimillionaires are 62 times more likely to serve in Congress than the average American, influencing tax and regulatory policy.

### Why it Matters
This research challenges the common perception that extreme wealth is concentrated solely among high-profile public figures or billionaires. By highlighting the massive influence of private business owners, the authors provide a clearer picture of economic inequality and the policy structures that facilitate significant wealth accumulation.

results.title: Fake iPhone Duo preorder page can steal crypto wallet data and more
results.author: Ben Lovejoy
results.content:
iPhone Duo pre-orders start on Friday, October 16, but scammers are trying to trick people into visiting a fake website to place their order now.
The website with the malware convincingly replicates the look of the real thing and claims to offer a $500 discount voucher as an “Authorized Partner Exclusive” …
Security researchers at Malwarebytes say the page uses the DarkSword exploit chain, which works with some older unpatched iPhones. You don’t have to do anything, just visiting the page is enough for the attack to launch.
Behind its Apple-style design and $500 voucher, the page uses the leaked DarkSword exploit chain to try to break into vulnerable iPhones. If it succeeds, a separate payload attempts to steal saved credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, and notes. You don’t have to fill in the form, tap a download, or approve anything. Opening the page is enough to start the attempt.
If it succeeds, then it captures your device identifier information and status and attempts to send a list of installed apps and the contents of your Apple Notes. Having done this, it turns its attention to crypto wallets.
The code looks for cryptocurrency wallets, including MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, Coinbase Wallet, Exodus, and Tonkeeper. It also attempts to recover saved credentials from the phone’s keychain. If it finds a targeted wallet and the first exchanges with its server succeed, it attempts to upload wallet files, recovered keychain data, and photo thumbnails. Exposure of wallet files or credentials could put funds at risk.
It goes on to try to access messages, contacts, call history, voicemail, email, calendar entries, and cached location data. The payload can also contact its server for further instructions.
The exploit chain was disclosed by Google back in March, with Apple issuing a patch later the same month.
9to5Mac’s Take
The usual advice applies to protect yourself. Never visit links sent to you unless you trust the sender and are specifically expecting them. Always ensure that you install iOS updates as soon as they are available.

results.summary:
Security researchers at Malwarebytes have identified a malicious website impersonating an official Apple store that uses the DarkSword exploit to compromise unpatched iPhones via a drive-by download.

### Key Points
- The fraudulent website lures users with a fake $500 discount voucher ahead of the official iPhone Duo pre-order date on October 16.
- Simply visiting the site triggers the DarkSword exploit chain, which targets vulnerabilities in older, unpatched versions of iOS.
- Once a device is compromised, the malware attempts to steal cryptocurrency wallet data, saved keychain credentials, and personal information like messages and contacts.
- The exploit chain was originally disclosed by Google in March, and Apple released a security patch to address the vulnerability later that same month.

### Why it Matters
This attack highlights the critical importance of keeping mobile devices updated with the latest security patches to defend against known exploit chains. Users should exercise extreme caution with unsolicited links, as drive-by attacks can compromise sensitive financial and personal data without requiring any user interaction.

results.title: Potato by air
results.author: Nathan Edwards
results.content:
The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B delivery drone weighs less than 15 pounds. It has 16 propellers — four for horizontal movement and 12 for vertical — a top speed of 60 miles per hour, a carrying capacity of up to 2.7 pounds, and a delivery radius of about 6 miles. It is authorized by the FAA for beyond-line-of-sight piloting. As a feat of engineering, it is impressive.
Potato by air
The day the dads in my neighborhood discovered drone delivery
Potato by air
The day the dads in my neighborhood discovered drone delivery
So far I’ve mostly used it to send people potatoes.
It all started a few Sunday mornings ago when my neighbor Will added me and a half dozen other local dads to a group chat. I only recognized a few of the numbers.
“Anyone looking for dumb stuff to entertain the kids?” he wrote, under a video of a drone lowering a blue doggie bag into his backyard. He’d discovered that we were now in the delivery range for drone service Wing’s partnership with Walmart, and could get household items dropped onto our lawns in 25 minutes. “Hopefully liquor store will get on board soon.”
Ever since I saw the video of an Amazon drone dropping a package in someone’s pool, I’ve needed to know one thing: Do you have to order drone delivery to your own yard? I raised the question in the chat.
Will, a few minutes later: “Nathan I just ordered you a potato to see if I can send to other people. 8 minutes out.”
Two minutes after that, a neighbor named Rick: “Will just want you to know you’re going to get your potato first.”
Rick and Will had each scanned the list of deliverable items — over 2,000 of them — and independently arrived at the same conclusion. “There is currently an air strike squadron of potatoes headed to our neighborhood,” Rick wrote.
At 12:14PM, a drone dropped a doggie bag in my yard. It contained a single russet potato and a bottle of water. Three minutes later, another arrived in Will’s yard, also containing a single potato and a bottle of water. (The water bottle seems to have been added as ballast; every Wing order I’ve placed came with one.)
Someone posted “The drones are everywhere.” Those of us who hadn’t met introduced ourselves. An apparently more practical dad named Jason ordered himself a pair of gloves. Dev, who lives in the next development over, was just out of drone range and could only watch in envy. Eventually, a storm rolled in and the potato drones tapered off.
My sixth grader turned our sky potato into oven fries; Will baked his.
The wild thing — aside from the fact that you can just order a drone delivery to someone else’s yard — is that each potato delivery cost 82 cents. Total. Each order came from the Walmart Supercenter a few miles away. Wing is absolutely losing money on this. There’s no minimum order, there’s no delivery fee, and the prices are the same as in-store. Wing’s not even collecting sales tax. Welcome back, millennial lifestyle subsidy!
At these prices, if you’re not using drones to send potatoes to your neighbors you’re leaving money on the table. That evening, I remembered that my friend Bill had been going through a rough time lately.
I sent him a potato.
Okay, technically, Wing’s terms of service state, “You will not use the Service to engage in any unlawful behavior, or to cause harassment, nuisance, annoyance or inconvenience to Wing, its users or any other person.” And I can definitely see ways you could abuse the system to do that.
While I lacked actual permission to land a drone potato in Bill’s yard, based on our relationship, I was confident I had spiritual permission. (This was confirmed a couple of days later when he asked me to drone deliver some candy for his kids. I sent the candy, and then another potato, and then the link to the Wing app.)
So what’s stopping someone from using this to harass people, beyond your own moral compass and the fact that they ask you not to? When I asked what safeguards the company had in place to prevent unauthorized deliveries, Wing spokesperson Jessie Poole-Strang wrote:
Wing has safely completed over 1 million residential drone deliveries, averaging thousands per day. Customers must be physically present for their first order, and every order requires a verified account and confirmation of a clear delivery zone. Just like traditional delivery or mailing a package, customers can choose to send an order to a friend or family member’s address that lives in eligible service areas. In the rare event a resident ever has a concern about a delivery to their property, our support team can help (support@wing.com).
Now, is drone delivery wasteful? If you’re only buying a single lightweight item — like a stick of deodorant, a bottle of sunscreen, or a potato — it seems more environmentally friendly than driving to the store. And as long as it’s subsidized, it’s way cheaper than DoorDash or whatever people use. I could see situations where it would be genuinely useful, especially if you can’t leave the house but you desperately need a bottle of ibuprofen and a Gatorade (for example). And of course it would be preposterous to DoorDash someone a single raw potato.
Of course, once you order more than a pound or so of stuff, that math goes off the rails. One afternoon, my wife ordered a box of frozen horchata mochi and a pint of gelato — among the few frozen desserts on the list. They arrived in two separate drones, three minutes apart, and each came with a small bottle of water. They held up surprisingly well during their seven-minute trips in the full Texas sun, considering the total lack of insulation. But it did feel silly to get two drones for two items.
That’s how they get you, of course. They hook you with convenience while hiding the true cost of the service. Drone delivery further squeezes gig workers in an already shrinking labor market, and it’s one more excuse for big companies to suppress wages. You don’t have to pay a drone, and you don’t have to tip it, either.
It’s been just over three weeks since we found out we had access to subsidized drone delivery. Aside from the two desserts and a couple of bags of Nerds Gummy Clusters, I’ve only used it to send potatoes to the dads. I sent three last week, plus one to myself to throw them off the scent. I’ve probably blown my cover now.
The other day someone — not me — escalated and sent Rick a broccoli potato soup. I’m pretty sure it was Will.
What have I learned from all of this? Well, I now know a few more people in my neighborhood. I’ve learned that drone delivery is way more useful to me than agentic AI has ever been. And that given the opportunity to airdrop subsidized potatoes to my friends, I’ll take it.
results.summary:
Wing’s Hummingbird 7000W-B drone, operating in partnership with Walmart, is currently providing low-cost, rapid residential delivery services that allow users to send small items to neighbors’ homes.

### Key Points
- The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B drone features 16 propellers, a 60 mph top speed, and a 2.7-pound carrying capacity.
- FAA-authorized beyond-line-of-sight operations enable Wing to deliver over 2,000 household items from local Walmart Supercenters.
- Current service models include no delivery fees or order minimums, with deliveries often arriving in under 30 minutes.
- Wing has completed over 1 million residential deliveries, requiring verified accounts and clear delivery zones for safety.
- The service allows users to send items to third-party addresses, provided the recipient is within an eligible service area.

### Why it Matters
This service represents a significant shift in last-mile logistics by offering highly subsidized, rapid delivery that bypasses traditional gig-economy labor costs. While the convenience is high, the model raises questions regarding long-term economic sustainability and the environmental impact of using multiple drones for small, individual item shipments.

results.title: I Visited Lightship’s AE.1 EV Travel Trailer, and Now I Want to Take an Off-the-Grid Road Trip
results.author: Omar Gallaga
results.content:
I’m approaching the age where I’m supposed to start desiring RV life. I’m not planning to retire anytime soon, but the older I get, the more appealing the idea of abandoning yard work, home repairs and geographic permanence for a life on the open road in a big old house on wheels becomes. My neighbors have an RV they park in the space between our houses, keeping both a permanent location and a home they can travel in; they still have yard work and house repairs, but few complaints.
So it was with some curiosity that I visited a pop-up for Lightship, a Colorado company making EV trailers for RV enthusiasts, outside the flagship Yeti outdoor-recreation store in Austin, Texas. The company’s eye-catching AE.1 trailer was parked and open to the public. (AE.1 refers to Aero-Electric 1.)
Lightship staffers handed out brochures, stickers and pins to visitors who climbed into the trailer, some of whom seemed surprised by the sleek, air-conditioned interior. The demo model boasted a cushioned lounge area, appliances including a hideaway dishwasher, microwave, full sink and stovetop, a full bathroom and shower area, and plenty of storage. It can sleep up to six.
More from CNET
The selling point of the highly customizable AE.1, which starts at $157,500, is that it offers a more modern design than most RVs and trailers. It includes thoughtful design touches and an electric-powered motor called TrekDrive that kicks in when in motion to lighten the load on whatever’s pulling the trailer. If it’s an EV truck or SUV, that could significantly extend the range between charges.
Pushing back on decades of RV design
Ben Parker, Lightship’s co-founder and chief commercial officer, worked at Tesla in California as a battery engineer and was inspired while traveling in an RV during the pandemic. Parker started the company with Toby Krauss, another former Tesla employee who worked in finance and product management and serves as Lightship’s CEO.
Parker said there’s a gigantic market of Americans who want to travel in camper RVs, but their options have been limited to a few highly consolidated manufacturers offering unchanging designs. So far, he said, customers interested in Lightship are a mix of EV owners and longtime enthusiasts who want “greater capacity, comfort and independence.”
“Our customers are people who love spending time outdoors and want more freedom in how they travel,” Parker said.
The AE.1’s most notable design feature is that it compresses from a 10-foot-tall Camp Mode with lots of windows and headroom to a Road Mode that lowers the roof to under 7 feet, making the AE.1 more aerodynamic in motion. Most of the trailer’s features, from the lighting to extras like an auto-leveling system and a motorized awning, are controlled by an app. A solar array on the trailer’s roof helps keep power flowing.
If you limit your A/C and power use, the AE.1 can last for about a week off the grid before it needs additional charging, Parker said. The AE.1 has hookups for EV charging as well as the kind of 220-volt hookups found at RV parks. It can hook up to external devices with vehicle-to-load power capabilities.
Some of the more interesting option features include a pull-down bed that attaches to the trailer’s ceiling and a setup for a 4K video projector that can be mounted inside the trailer for viewing on a pull-down screen.
“The demand we’ve seen reflects a broader appetite for innovation in the RV space,” Parker said. “Customers are excited by the idea of an RV that combines modern technology, energy independence and a dramatically improved towing experience in a single product.”
The co-founder said his company wants the buying and using experience of an AE.1 to wow customers enough for Lightship to gain a foothold in a market that’s not very open to newcomers.
“Breaking into any established industry requires earning trust,” he said. “We’ve focused on building a high-quality product that solves real customer pain points and delivering an experience that people can immediately appreciate once they see it and use it for themselves.”
New trailer players
Lightship is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It’s expanding its manufacturing center there to accommodate additional trailer production, as well as production of a carriage-minus-trailer product called PowerSled, which it’s been selling to businesses like movie productions that need a mobile platform with electric power.
Lightship’s mission to disrupt the RV market is not unlike that of another company, Pebble, that has also been making EV trailers in California.
Parker said the main difference between Lightship and Pebble is that Lightship is sourcing more of its materials domestically. Parker estimates that about 75% of the materials used to make an AE.1 are sourced domestically, and all assembly is done in-house.
Pebble, however, is undercutting Lightship on price. Lightship originally planned to offer a lower-priced $125,000 base model without the self-propelled TrekDrive motor. However, the company has since changed its strategy, moving to a single standard base price with a standard 77 kWh battery and various add-on options and upgrades.
Possible retirement plans
For me, a non-RV person, the AE.1 feels design-forward and includes features like a built-in auto-hitch, an auto-leveler, and lots of charging ports and stations, all of which appeal to someone like me who has no idea what they’re doing. The interior feels spacious, but not so much that it makes the exterior look oversized. The ability to shrink down to a smaller size — the AE.1 performs safety checks before compressing to ensure windows aren’t open and nothing will break — brings the wow factor.
It doesn’t take much time in the trailer to imagine traveling in it and using Lightship’s trailer as a mobile workstation (satellite internet service is not included, but it can be hooked up).
The AE.1 isn’t cheap, but it might be worth putting on the retirement wish list. You will still have to wait: the company’s waitlist for delivery is currently about a year long.
Lightship began shipping AE.1 trailers last year and said it expects to produce about 30 over the rest of this year. By sometime in 2027, with its expanded factory floor, it plans to ramp that up to 40 per month.
If you want to check out the AE.1 for yourself, the company maintains showrooms north of Denver and in San Francisco and will host a pop-up event in Las Vegas in late November.
results.summary:
Colorado-based startup Lightship is modernizing the recreational vehicle industry with its AE.1, an aerodynamic, electric-powered travel trailer designed to improve towing efficiency and offer off-grid energy independence.

### Key Points
- The AE.1 trailer features the TrekDrive electric motor, which assists towing vehicles to extend the range of electric trucks and SUVs.
- The unit utilizes a telescoping design that compresses from a 10-foot-tall "Camp Mode" to a sub-7-foot "Road Mode" for improved aerodynamics.
- Base models start at $157,500 and include a 77 kWh battery, solar roof array, and an app-controlled system for lighting and leveling.
- Founded by former Tesla engineers Ben Parker and Toby Krauss, the company sources approximately 75% of its materials domestically.
- Lightship is currently expanding its Broomfield, Colorado, manufacturing facility to increase production capacity from 30 units this year to 40 per month by 2027.

### Why it Matters
Lightship represents a significant shift toward electrification and modern design in a traditionally stagnant RV market dominated by legacy manufacturers. By integrating advanced battery technology and domestic manufacturing, the company aims to attract a new demographic of tech-focused travelers seeking sustainable, high-performance alternatives to conventional campers.

results.title: FBI hunting the hackers who stole its employees' sensitive data
results.author: Jenna McLaughlin
results.content:
FBI hunting the hackers who stole its employees' sensitive data
In a video posted on social media, the assistant director of the FBI's cyber division, Brett Leatherman, vowed Tuesday to hunt down the members of a cybercriminal group going by the name of ShinyHunters, the same group that last week claimed to steal reams of sensitive data from the FBI itself.
"You know how to find us, and we know how to find you," Leatherman said in the video, encouraging the prolific group of loosely connected data extortionists to come forward and share information or face the consequences. "I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours."
The FBI says it is "aggressively" investigating the breach and how hackers got ahold of sensitive FBI employment information, including whether the hackers got into third-party software or the FBI's own internal systems. In a statement emailed to NPR, a FBI spokesperson said the bureau is working "around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted."
It's still unclear how much information was stolen, though media organizations and threat intelligence researchers have already verified the authenticity of some of the stolen materials. Meanwhile, a defacement message was posted on the FBI's jobs website late last week where ShinyHunters took credit for the attack, and the site was temporarily taken down.
Current and former FBI employees familiar with the matter, who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because they feared reprisal for speaking about an ongoing investigation, said many employees first found out about the breach from media reports. They suggested there could be as many as several terabytes of text files in the data tranche, including FBI job applications, details on promotions, information on sensitive job postings, family details, medical data and more. Those same employees, particularly those who have retired, say there's growing frustration with FBI leadership, including FBI Director Kash Patel, about the lack of communication about the breach, exactly who is impacted, and how the FBI plans to protect its current and former employees. Some retired employees who worked undercover might need protection services like relocation assistance or even name changes if their data is exposed publicly.
The FBI told NPR it sent multiple "bureau wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting" of the breach" and that "the FBI treats the security of its own information and the safety of its workforce as top priorities."
One former senior FBI official told NPR the breach could be on par with the 2015 compromise of tens of millions of sensitive government employee records from the Office of Personnel Management. The U.S. government attributed that breach to the Chinese government and described it as a widespread espionage operation designed to identify potential targets for intelligence gathering.
However, unlike the OPM breach, there is more concern in this instance that the stolen materials will fall into the wrong hands or be otherwise weaponized, either by ShinyHunters or any number of criminal, terrorist, or nation-state organizations seeking to pilfer the stolen files. ShinyHunters has come out and said it never intended to leak the files, despite giving a deadline of Sept. 30 for the FBI to amend previously published press releases about the group that it argued were inaccurate, but that doesn't necessarily prevent further theft or exploitation of the data.
The bureau and its former employees are "bracing for impact" and assume that the stolen materials may be irretrievably compromised, according to the former senior FBI official.
But experts argue that the ShinyHunters members, which many threat intelligence researchers have previously identified as a loose collective of young hackers around the world, should also brace themselves for the FBI's response.
Cynthia Kaiser, the former FBI deputy director of the cyber division who currently leads ransomware research at cybersecurity company Halcyon, described the hackers as "reckless" for targeting the FBI, particularly knowing the FBI has a clear policy of not paying a ransom or negotiating with criminal actors. "When any threat actor targets the FBI directly, they should expect that the FBI is going to marshall additional resources to bring them quickly to justice," she wrote in a social media post.
While the FBI has promised to seek the information to make arrests against ShinyHunters hackers in the wake of this breach, it's unclear how imminent those actions might be.
The FBI's video posted on social media also featured a recently announced arrest of one alleged member of ShinyHunters in Amsterdam by the Dutch National Police, an operation the FBI thanked its Dutch partners for leading. However, that arrest preceded the ShinyHunters theft of FBI personnel data, according to the former senior FBI official familiar with the matter. It's unclear if that arrest served as motivation for the breach of FBI data and whether there was concern about potential retaliation following that arrest.
While the FBI has not shared any technical details about how the hackers got into its systems, Google's Mandiant published new research revealing that ShinyHunters is currently targeting a vulnerability in a human resources software tool called PeopleSoft, which is owned by tech giant Oracle. PeopleSoft is a tool used by the FBI, among other major clients in IT services, corporations, government, academia and beyond.
Google originally disclosed information about the vulnerability and its exploitation in June and revealed that while the company released a patch, some customers instead implemented protections like a firewall to attempt to prevent bad actors from exploiting it. Ultimately, ShinyHunters has managed to easily bypass those controls.
results.summary:
The FBI has launched an aggressive investigation into the cybercriminal group ShinyHunters after the hackers breached the FBIJobs.gov portal and stole sensitive personnel data from the bureau.

### Key Points
- The cybercriminal group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the breach, which potentially exposed terabytes of sensitive FBI employee data.
- Stolen information reportedly includes job applications, medical records, promotion details, and sensitive family information.
- Mandiant research indicates the hackers may have exploited a vulnerability in Oracle’s PeopleSoft human resources software used by the FBI.
- FBI Assistant Director Brett Leatherman publicly vowed to track down the hackers, warning them to come forward before facing legal consequences.
- The breach has caused significant concern among current and former employees regarding the potential weaponization of their personal data by criminal or state actors.

### Why it Matters
This breach represents a major security failure that could compromise the safety of undercover personnel and sensitive government operations. The incident highlights the persistent vulnerability of federal agencies to data extortion and the significant risks posed when third-party software tools are exploited by sophisticated criminal collectives.

results.title: "That's so AI" is the new insult, and it means bullshit
results.author: Gail Sherman
results.content:
Gen Alpha's slang makes it clear what kids think of so-called artificial intelligence. As reported by the Guardian, the most savage burn a young person can hurl at you is "That's AI" or "That's so AI."
The kids – gen Alpha – have noticed that certain qualities of AI-generated slop, such as the way it's superficially convincing but ultimately cheap and of dubious value, can be found in lots of other things: knock-off merchandise, exaggerated claims, excuses your parents make. If something is considered somehow suspect, then it is also, by definition, AI.
Unlike 6-7 and skibidi, which were mostly nonsense designed to confuse and possibly aggravate old folks, "That's so AI" is social commentary disguised as substitute profanity. For the companies that have spent billions on chatbots and image generators that spew nonsense, it has to sting when their product becomes a synonym for bullshit. But sometimes it takes a kid to point out that the emperor has no clothes.
More about Gen Alpha slang:
Boing Boing has covered a twelve-minute primer on Gen Alpha slang, the largest dictionary of English-language slang, now free online, and a 1788 dictionary of vulgar slang.
results.summary:
Generation Alpha is increasingly using the phrase "That's so AI" as a derogatory slang term to describe anything perceived as cheap, inauthentic, or lacking genuine human value.

### Key Points
- Gen Alpha uses "That's so AI" to label knock-off merchandise, exaggerated claims, or insincere behavior as suspect.
- The term functions as social commentary, contrasting with previous nonsense-based slang like "skibidi" or "6-7."
- The phrase reflects a growing cultural skepticism toward the quality and reliability of artificial intelligence products.
- Linguistic experts note this shift as a modern evolution of slang that serves as a substitute for profanity.

### Why it Matters
This linguistic trend signals a significant branding challenge for technology companies investing billions into generative AI tools. When a product name becomes synonymous with low-quality "slop," it highlights a disconnect between corporate marketing and public perception among younger demographics.

results.title: WPBeginner Spotlight 28: WPVibe Hits 40,000 Sites, a New WPForms Dashboard, and Two WordPress Security Updates
results.author: Editorial Staff
results.content:
September was the month WordPress plugins really started talking to AI assistants in a serious way. You can now manage backups, forms, online stores, and fundraising campaigns just by asking Claude or ChatGPT, and there’s a good chance you already have some of these plugins installed.
WordPress shipped two security releases and WooCommerce shipped two more, so please update before you read the rest.
As always, we’ll walk you through what happened, why it matters, and how you can use it on your own site.
WPBeginner Spotlight brings you a monthly roundup of the most important WordPress news, updates, and community happenings.
Got something to share? Whether it’s a new product launch, a significant update, or an exciting event, reach out to us through our contact form, and your news could be featured in the next edition!
WPVibe Passes 40,000 Installs, Launches Fleet Management, and Learns Six More Plugins
WPVibe is a free WordPress MCP plugin that connects your WordPress site to AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor. You simply describe what you want in plain language, and the AI takes care of the work on your site.
The plugin crossed 40,000 active installs on September 23, just two weeks after hitting 20,000, and its WordPress.org rating sits at 5 out of 5.
Syed Balkhi shared the milestone along with a list of everything the team shipped in one week. The biggest addition to WPVibe is the new Fleet Management feature.
If you manage more than one WordPress site, you can now ask your AI assistant which updates are pending across all of them and then run those updates from a single chat.
Here is what makes it different from a typical site manager tool. WPVibe checks every site before and after each update to make sure the update was completed successfully and the site is still working as expected.
WordPress core updates stay out unless you include them, and even then, the job pauses for your approval. If one site runs into an issue, the others keep going.
You can even close the tab while the job is running. The updates continue in the background and finish on their own. Fleet Management is included with every WPVibe plan, including the free plan. The plans differ only in how many AI actions you can run each day, not in which features you get.
Another important development is the growing list of plugins your AI can now understand. These integrations use the WordPress Abilities API, a standard that lets plugins describe what they can do in a format AI assistants can understand.
WPVibe tests each integration and publishes ready-to-use prompts, which it calls recipes. Here’s what was added in September:
- All in One SEO: You can ask which posts are missing a meta description and have the AI write one based on the post content. 13 SEO operations work in the free version.
- WPForms: You can build a contact form from a single sentence, or ask the AI to improve the labels and required fields on a form you already have. Five of the six recipes work with WPForms Lite.
- WPCode: Instead of only writing new snippets, the AI can now see which code snippet failed, on which line, and on which page.
- Easy Digital Downloads: You can pull sales reports, create discount codes, and add new products from one chat. We cover this in more detail below.
- PushEngage: You can create subscriber segments, check your setup, and send a push notification once you’ve approved the exact text.
- Duplicator: The AI can take a backup before it touches a plugin update and will wait until the backup is complete before continuing.
- SVG uploads: WPVibe 1.19 lets your AI add SVG logos and icons to the media library. It strips scripts from every file first, since embedded scripts are the reason WordPress blocks SVG uploads by default.
Along with these integrations, a new four-step setup page arrived in wp-admin. It tests the connection from both inside and outside your site.
If something is blocking the connection, such as a security plugin that has disabled application passwords, the page tells you exactly what to fix in plain language.
We believe this is where WordPress management is heading. The AI assistant you already talk to every day is becoming the place where you run your website.
WPForms Launches a Dashboard That Shows Every Form’s Entries, Payments, and Views in One Place
WPForms is the most popular drag and drop form builder for WordPress, used on more than 6 million websites. On September 17, it gained a new Dashboard that shows how every form on your site is doing the moment you log in.
Until now, you had to open each form separately to see how it was performing. The new Dashboard puts all of them side by side, so you can quickly see where activity is growing and which form needs your attention next.
Here’s what you’ll see on the Dashboard:
- Site-wide numbers: Stat cards for forms, entries, payments, views, and spam, each one a single figure for your whole site.
- An entries feed: A chart of activity over your chosen date range, with a table listing every form alongside its entries, views, and conversion rate.
- Payment totals: Daily payment totals with summary cards for sales and subscriptions.
- Top visitor locations: The countries your form entries come from.
- Next steps: Suggested addons and integrations based on how you use WPForms. These change as your setup grows.
There’s nothing to install or configure. The Dashboard opens as soon as you click WPForms in your admin menu, and it’s included with every plan, including the free WPForms Lite.
One more addition arrived just after our last issue. WPForms QR Code creates a scannable code for any form, and a visitor at an event or in your shop can open the form on their phone with one scan.
WordPress 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 Fix 12 Security Issues, and the Roadmap to WordPress 7.2 Is Out
Two WordPress releases arrived within a week of each other, and both of them matter for your site’s security. If you have automatic updates turned off, update today, but take a full backup first.
WordPress 7.1.1 landed on September 17 with 17 fixes in core, 19 fixes in the block editor, and 11 security fixes. Rafie Muhammad from Awesome Motive reported one of those security issues.
WordPress 7.1.2 followed on September 22 with a single fix for a critical vulnerability. Under certain server and theme conditions, an attacker without a login could trick WordPress into loading a local PHP file.
The core team backported the fix all the way back to WordPress 4.7, so older sites are protected as well. Looking ahead, the team also published the Roadmap to WordPress 7.2.
The release is planned for early December 2026. Here’s what the team is working on, though as with every roadmap, not everything will make it into the final release.
- Notes get suggestions and reactions: The collaboration notes introduced in 7.1 are expanding to include suggested edits and emoji reactions.
- Sudo mode: WordPress will ask you to confirm your password before sensitive actions, similar to how your bank does.
- Secrets API: A safer place for plugins to store API keys and credentials.
- Table of Contents and Description List blocks: Two long-requested blocks that you’ll be able to use without a plugin.
- A new default theme: The team has proposed a minimal blog theme called Ipsum, and default themes will move away from year-based names.
AI features will stay in the official AI plugin for now. The team’s position is that AI needs to show clear adoption and value before it moves into core, and we think that’s the right call.
Duplicator Brings AI Backups, AutoTune, and Pro’s Backup Engine to the Free Plugin
Duplicator is a WordPress backup and migration plugin with more than 1 million active installs. On September 22, the team called Duplicator 5.0 the biggest update it has ever released.
One of the biggest new features is AI-powered backups. Duplicator now uses the WordPress Abilities API to give connected AI assistants three backup-related actions.
Your AI assistant can list existing backups, create a full or database-only backup, and check whether a backup has finished. That may sound simple, but it adds an important safety step to AI workflows.
Before your assistant updates a plugin or makes changes across dozens of posts, it can create a backup first. The feature is available in the free plugin and requires WordPress 6.9 or later.
The rest of the release is just as practical:
- AutoTune: When a backup fails, the fix is usually a single setting, but most people don’t know which one. AutoTune runs real test backups on your server and adjusts the setting that caused the failure until a backup succeeds. You’ll find it under Tools » AutoTune.
- Duplicator Cloud for Lite: Free users can now store backups off-site in Duplicator’s own cloud storage, with no Pro license or third-party account needed. You can restore from the cloud even when your server is completely down.
- One engine for Lite and Pro: Both versions now run on the same backup engine, so free users get the same reliability improvements as Pro.
- One-click restore and encryption: Restore your site from inside wp-admin, and protect backup files with a password.
- Server Overview: A pass or fail panel for worker mode, loopback requests, and PHP time and memory limits, with advice when something needs attention.
Backups are one of those things most site owners set up once and never think about again. Duplicator 5.0 makes that first setup far less likely to fail, which is where most backup problems start.
Easy Digital Downloads Now Works With Claude and ChatGPT: Sales Reports, Discount Codes, and New Products From One Chat
Easy Digital Downloads is the plugin for selling digital products like ebooks, software, and music in WordPress. The free version has more than 40,000 active installs, and paid plans add features like recurring payments and software licensing.
On September 23, the team announced that Easy Digital Downloads now works with an AI assistant. Version 3.7.1 adds 25 abilities that cover orders, customers, products, discounts, sales reports, email and download logs, and store settings.
In practice, this means you can ask Claude or ChatGPT for last month’s sales report, including refunds and average order value. You can also ask for a discount code with a start date, end date, and usage limit, and the AI will create it as inactive so you can review it before it goes live.
You can even hand the AI a list of finished products, and it will add them as drafts with descriptions already written, ready for you to attach the files.
Customer support gets easier too. When a customer says their download never arrived, the AI can look up the order, the receipt log, and the download log in one go.
You’ll find the setting under Downloads » Tools » AI. Read and write access are separate, so you decide whether the AI can only report on your store or also make changes to it.
Running a store used to mean filling in the same forms over and over. With this release, you can hand off the repetitive half of the job while still keeping the final approval for yourself.
Charitable Lets AI Assistants Create Fundraisers and Log Donations, and Adds Tiered Rates for Fee Relief
Charitable is a donation and fundraising plugin for WordPress, with a free Lite version and paid plans for nonprofits that need recurring gifts, peer-to-peer campaigns, and more. It had a busy September.
The biggest update is that AI assistants can now create fundraisers and manage donations. You can type a single sentence into ChatGPT or Claude, and a draft campaign appears inside Charitable’s drag-and-drop builder.
The AI builds the campaign from a template, with suggested donation amounts already scaled to the fundraising goal you mentioned. And campaigns are just the start.
You can also log a donation that arrived as a check in the mail, add a new donor to your records, or add a required dropdown field to an existing donation form. This is a Charitable Pro feature, and anything the AI creates is saved as a draft for you to review first.
The second update is Tiered Rates for Fee Relief. If you’re not familiar with it, Fee Relief asks donors a simple question at checkout: would they like to cover the processing fee?
Until now, that question used a single rate for each payment gateway, which doesn’t always make sense. A $10 gift and a $500 gift don’t feel the same to the donor.
You can now set up donation bands, each with its own percentage and fixed fee, plus an optional maximum. The setting lives under Charitable » Settings » Advanced » Fee Relief on the Plus plan and higher.
Charitable also shipped three smaller releases:
- Visual Automation Builder: Build donor follow-ups as a trigger, conditions, and ordered actions on a drag-and-drop canvas.
- Windcave recurring donations: Monthly giving for nonprofits in New Zealand and Australia using the Windcave gateway.
- Beacon templates in Charitable Lite: More ready-made campaign designs, now in the free version.
Universally Adds Automatic Language Redirects, and BuddyBoss Now Translates What Members Write
Universally is an AI translation service that translates your website into 110+ languages automatically. There’s a free plan, and paid plans are priced per site.
Universally for WordPress 1.0.9 arrived on September 17, and the main addition is automatic language redirects. So if a visitor’s browser is set to Portuguese and they open your English homepage, they land directly on the Portuguese version without having to find a language switcher.
Visitors still stay in control. If they switch to another language, Universally remembers that choice for 30 days, so nobody gets stuck in a translation they don’t want.
The release also gives you more control over how Google treats your translations. You can now tell search engines whether a translation is meant for French speakers everywhere or only for visitors in France, without having to touch the hreflang tags yourself.
There’s related news for community sites too, because BuddyBoss now integrates with Universally. Most translation plugins only translate the pages you publish. This integration translates what your members write as well.
That means a Spanish-speaking member and an English-speaking member can read each other’s posts and comments in real time. For a community that spans several countries, that removes the biggest barrier to conversation.
ConsentLayer Releases Cookie Inspector, a Free Chrome Extension That Shows Exactly Which Cookies Your Site Sets
ConsentLayer is a cookie consent solution for websites that people build and manage with AI tools. You can ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Cursor to install it, and it will set up the right consent rules for each region.
The free plan covers most small websites. This month the team released Cookie Inspector, a free Chrome extension.
Open any page, and it shows you which cookies are set, when they were set, and which script set them. The really useful part is the consent check.
Click Accept on your own cookie banner, and Cookie Inspector shows you exactly which cookies that click released. If a tracking cookie shows up before anyone has accepted, then your banner isn’t doing its job.
It works with any cookie banner, not just ConsentLayer’s. If you’ve ever wondered whether your consent setup actually works, this is a quick way to find out.
WooCommerce 11.1 Puts Variation Galleries in Core and Adds Order Withdrawal, With Two Security Releases and 11.2 Beta Following
WooCommerce released version 11.1 on September 1 with 561 changes from 77 contributors. Three changes stand out for store owners.
- Variation image galleries: Each product variation can now have its own set of images, right in core. This replaces the Additional Variation Images extension, and your existing images migrate automatically.
- Right to order withdrawal: Customers in the EU can cancel an order within the 14-day window the law gives them, right from their account.
- Faster Store API and REST requests: Variable product pages and block registration both got performance improvements.
Two security releases followed the main release. WooCommerce 11.1.1 arrived on September 18 and also fixed a Mini-Cart bug, and 11.1.2 came on September 22 with a fix for a loop in the new variation galleries that affected some themes.
If you haven’t updated to 11.1.2 yet, please do so now. Next up is WooCommerce 11.2, now in beta and scheduled for the week of October 6.
It brings editable order withdrawal emails, a product CSV importer that matches existing products by barcode, date fields at checkout for birthdays and delivery dates, and sticky product filters. There’s also a new theme worth keeping an eye on.
Purple is WooCommerce’s first official block theme, back in public beta after a pause, with ten color palettes, ten font pairings, and a pattern library built for stores. It’s on GitHub for now and will come to the WordPress theme directory once testing is complete.
QuickSnip Adds a Loom Importer So You Can Move Your Whole Video Library
QuickSnip is the screen recording and screenshot tool that our founder Syed Balkhi built with his college roommate, and we covered it when it launched last month.
It records in 4K with AI captions and gives you a shareable link the moment you stop recording. Paid plans start at $6 per month.
Several people asked whether they could bring their old Loom recordings over, so the team built a Loom importer. Just connect your Loom account, and your whole library moves over, so switching doesn’t mean losing years of walkthroughs.
If your existing library was the only thing keeping you on Loom, that reason is gone.
In Other News
PushEngage, the web push notification and customer engagement platform, launched free Chrome and Firefox extensions. Open any page on your site, and the extension uses AI to draft a push notification from the page content, ready to target and schedule without opening the dashboard.
OptinMonster, the popup and lead generation toolkit, added Campaign Teasers on Plus plans and higher. A popup, fullscreen campaign, or floating bar can now start as a small tab at the edge of the screen. When a visitor closes the campaign, it shrinks back into that tab instead of disappearing for the rest of their visit.
Agencies also get Analytics Exports to CSV on Pro and Growth plans. The export covers the campaigns, date range, and columns you choose.
Smash Balloon, the social feeds plugin family, had a busy month. Reviews Feed Pro can now pull your Airbnb reviews onto your own booking page, and Feed Analytics Pro 2.0 shows which review and which post earns clicks.
You can also set up Facebook Events feeds from your own Facebook app. The Instagram plugin now warns you when a feed stops updating.
Sugar Calendar, the event calendar plugin, added Registration Forms. You can ask ticket buyers and RSVP guests custom questions such as meal choice, shirt size, or workshop track, either before or after checkout. The answers are saved on the attendee record right next to their ticket.
Thrive Themes rebuilt Thrive Leads, its opt-in form plugin, from the ground up with a new dashboard, a form wizard, and a My Forms screen. Everything you already built carries over.
Thrive Apprentice, its course plugin, now shows students the exact date their next lesson unlocks. It can also drip whole chapters at once.
WPConsent, the WordPress privacy compliance plugin, introduced Banner Analytics in version 1.1.9. It shows how many visitors saw your cookie banner and left without making a choice, which gives you an idea of how much of your traffic your analytics never sees.
The plugin also passed 200,000 installs at the end of August. That is double the 100,000 it celebrated last November.
All in One SEO extended its TruSEO content score to category and tag pages in version 5.0.1. Category and tag archives often rank well, yet site owners rarely optimize them, so this closes a gap that many sites have.
Uncanny Automator, the no-code automation plugin, shipped versions 7.5 and 7.6 with FluentCart, FluentBoards, All-in-One WP Migration, Really Simple Security, and Site Kit by Google integrations. Everyone on the free Automator Lite plan now gets starter access to Uncanny Agent, its AI assistant.
Pretty Links, the link shortener for WordPress, launched a UTM Builder. You fill in the campaign, source, and medium, and Pretty Links builds the tracking parameters for you while keeping the shared link short and branded.
Advanced Coupons, the coupon toolkit for WooCommerce, added Tiered Cart Discounts. One coupon can hold several spend thresholds, and the cart automatically applies the highest tier it reaches.
Customers can also now redeem loyalty points for products and coupons. Tiered Cart Discounts requires the Premium version.
BuddyBoss, the community platform for WordPress, shipped Email Digest, the most requested feature on its roadmap. Members can choose daily or weekly notification summaries instead of getting one email per event. It’s included on the Start plan and higher.
StoreAgent, an AI platform for WooCommerce stores from the WPBeginner Growth Fund family, now lets you connect Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor to your store. The connection uses MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, which is the standard that AI assistants use to talk to outside tools.
You can ask for today’s orders, have the AI write missing product descriptions, or create a coupon from a single sentence. You approve the connection from your own store and choose between read-only and read-and-write access.
aThemes released a Delivery and Pickup module in Merchant Pro, its WooCommerce toolkit. Shoppers choose Shipping, Pickup, or Delivery and pick a date and time slot, the same flow they know from large retailers.
HeroThemes added Views to Heroic Inbox, its shared inbox plugin. Views are saved filters that organize a busy support inbox so agents find the right tickets to answer next.
WordPress.org published a free AI-Powered WordPress course on Learn WordPress. It walks through connecting an AI provider, using the editorial AI tools, and building your own abilities.
If all the AI news above has made you curious, this course is a good place to start, and it’s free.
WooCommerce also published its own version of Anthropic’s open-source Claude Commerce Agent. A shopping assistant builds a cart and hands the customer to the normal checkout, while a merchant assistant answers questions about sales and stock.
Every change the merchant assistant proposes waits for your approval. The project is still experimental, so it’s not ready for live stores yet.
Mary Hubbard, the WordPress Executive Director, is now president of the Open Website Alliance. The alliance brings together the communities behind Drupal, Joomla, TYPO3, and WordPress to advocate for open source on the web.
Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com and WooCommerce, launched Spacefast, a hosting service it describes as a home for what your agent makes. You publish a static site or a supported app straight from a conversation with an AI agent.
Spacefast is not WordPress hosting, but it shows where the company thinks website building is going.
New Tools & Plugins
- WPVibe: Free WordPress MCP plugin, now with Fleet Management and more integrations.
- Cookie Inspector by ConsentLayer: A free Chrome extension that shows which cookies a page sets, which script set them, and whether your consent banner holds them back.
- QuickSnip: Screen recording tool with 4K video, easy editing, shareable links, and now a built-in Loom importer.
That’s everything for this month. There are two security updates to install, a backup plugin that tunes itself, and a long list of plugins that now take instructions from your AI assistant.
If there’s a story or a plugin you think we should cover in the next issue, we’d love to hear about it. Reach out through our contact form, and we’ll see you in the next Spotlight.
If you liked this article, then please subscribe to our YouTube Channel for WordPress video tutorials. You can also find us on Twitter and Facebook.

- WPVibe surpassed 40,000 installs and introduced Fleet Management, enabling users to run updates across multiple WordPress sites from a single AI chat.
